opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about the next stage of Aya, a lot of the hardest problems are optimization problems in disguise.

The first is the trade-off you face when you train one model across many languages. People call it the "curse of multilinguality." As you add more languages to a fixed-capacity model, performance on some of them starts to degrade. Languages compete for capacity, and the high-resource ones tend to win. So one big question is how to allocate capacity and data across languages more intelligently. That could mean better data weighting, curriculum strategies, or architectures that route computation differently depending on the input. We want gains for lower-resource languages without paying for them with English or other widely spoken languages.

The second is data. For many of the languages we care about, there just isn't much high-quality data. A lot of what exists is machine-translated, and translation artifacts can creep in. So we're very interested in what you could call data optimization: arbitrage across multiple teacher models, synthetic data generation that stays culturally and linguistically grounded, and smarter pruning, so we're not just training on more data but on the right data. In my experience, how you shape the data distribution often matters more than squeezing another trick out of the optimizer.

The third is efficiency. Much of the world that would benefit most from multilingual models doesn't have access to huge compute. So it matters to us that these models work well when they're smaller, quantized, or compressed. My older research showed that compression doesn't hurt all parts of the distribution equally. The long tail, which often includes underrepresented languages, tends to get hit hardest. So a key question is how to make models efficient without quietly sacrificing the communities we set out to serve.

Finally, there's preference training and safety across languages. Most alignment work has been done in English, and it doesn't transfer cleanly. Optimizing for human preferences and for harm mitigation in a way that respects local context, rather than imposing one view, is still very much an open problem.

So it's less one optimization challenge and more a set of them. The common thread is making sure the benefits of progress reach everyone, not just the languages that already dominate the internet.

r002.rationale: It says English-based alignment does not transfer cleanly, but does not raise whether preference data from a subset of Aya’s 101 languages transfers across the others.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that Aya has gotten us a long way on the data side, right? We now have this massive multilingual instruction dataset, over a hundred languages, built with thousands of contributors around the world. And that was really the first bottleneck. But what I've become increasingly convinced of is that data alone doesn't solve the problem, because the way we optimize these models is still fundamentally biased toward high-resource languages.

So there are a few things I think about. The first is just the training recipe itself. When you do preference tuning or RLHF, almost all the signal is coming from English preference data. And what we see is that you can actually degrade performance in other languages, or you get this kind of uneven alignment where the model is safe and helpful in English and much less so in, say, Swahili or Bengali. So one challenge is: how do you do multilingual preference optimization in a way that actually transfers, and that doesn't just treat the other languages as an afterthought you bolt on at the end?

The second is tokenization, which I think is a hugely underrated problem. A lot of languages are penalized before any learning even happens, because the tokenizer fragments them into many more tokens. That means they're more expensive to serve, they get less effective context, and the model is just learning a worse representation. I'd love for us to think more seriously about optimizing for efficiency across languages, not just average efficiency measured on English benchmarks.

And then the third thing, which is maybe more of a research agenda than a single challenge, is evaluation. Right now, a lot of our multilingual evals are translated versions of English tests, and that's not really measuring what we care about. If we're going to optimize for something, we have to be able to measure it. So I'd say the next stage for Aya is really about moving from "do we have the data" to "are our optimization and measurement choices actually serving the people who speak these languages." That's where I want the community to go.

r001.rationale: It identifies tokenization as a challenge because some languages are fragmented into more tokens, but it does not specify languages written in non-Latin scripts.

r002.rationale: It asks how preference optimization based largely on English preference data can transfer across languages, and notes Aya’s dataset covers over a hundred languages.

astra-6.text:
One of the challenges I’d like Aya to tackle is how we improve performance across languages without simply optimizing for the languages where we have the most data. If you look only at an average score, you can miss that some communities are benefiting much less than others. How do we make those tradeoffs visible and use them to guide training?

There’s also the question of efficiency. Can we get better multilingual coverage without continually increasing the size and cost of the model? That matters because supporting a language is only part of accessibility; people also need to be able to use the model. I’d like us to think about quality across languages and the resources required to deliver that quality together.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the big challenges is understanding the trade-offs in multilingual models. When we improve performance in one language, what happens to the others? How do we make sure that languages with less data benefit, rather than having the optimization dominated by the languages that are already well represented?

And that raises a question about what we’re optimizing for. An average score across languages can hide enormous differences in the quality of someone’s experience. I’d like us to get better at measuring those differences and using that signal to guide how we balance data and training. The goal is to make progress across languages, especially where the gap is greatest.
